analysis.title: Chase Spending Data Updated Through October 29, 2026
key_insights: October total Chase card spending is up about 5.7% Y/Y month-to-date through Oct. 29, down from about 6.8% in September. Discretionary growth slowed to 5.3% from 6.9%, while non-discretionary growth edged up to 6.8% from 6.6%.
Total spending excluding gas stations is up 4.9% Y/Y MTD through Oct. 29, against 6.1% in September. Trailing 12-month growth is about 4.50% for total spending and 4.26% excluding gas.
Growth slowed across all three income cohorts. Upper income is at 7.0% (from 8.0%), middle income at 7.4% (from 8.5%) and lower income at 5.4% (from 7.0%).

Discretionary spending slowed in every income cohort. Lower income eased to 5.3% from 7.3%, middle to 7.4% from 9.0% and upper to 6.9% from 8.4%. Non-discretionary growth was lower for lower income (5.7% from 6.2%) and middle income (7.4% from 7.5%), and slightly higher for upper income (7.3% from 7.2%).

Gen Z and Millennial spending is up about 8.8% Y/Y MTD, down from 9.7% in September, and still the fastest-growing cohort. Part of that gap reflects life-cycle effects, since income and spending rise fastest early in a career. Gen X slowed to 4.2% and Baby Boomers to 1.8%.

Within the younger cohort, discretionary growth slowed to 8.5% from 9.8% while non-discretionary growth rose to 9.9% from 9.4%. Gen X discretionary growth fell to 3.7% from 5.3% and Boomers to 0.9% from 3.0%. The slowdown was concentrated in hobby, home and travel spending.
JPMorgan suspects part of the M/M discretionary slowdown comes from the Labor Day weekend moving from the last week of August to the first week of September.

Gas station and other energy goods spending is up about 26.8% Y/Y MTD, accelerating from 24.6% in September. JPMorgan estimates average gas prices are up about 40.2% Y/Y, at roughly $4.32 a gallon in October versus $4.35 in September. It sees spending at the pump as a regressive headwind for lower and middle income consumers.

By PCE category, non-durable goods spending growth slowed to 7.4% from 8.2% in September, the YTD peak, reflecting pass-through of higher energy prices. Durable goods slowed to 3.3% from 6.0% and services to about 5.1% from 6.0%.
In Gen X, non-discretionary growth rose slightly to 5.4% from 5.3%. In Boomers it fell to 3.8% from 4.2%.

The appendix is a schema of the full Chase spending dataset, covering PCE, NAICS, proprietary discretionary/non-discretionary categories and ratio families, each sliceable by generation, income and card presence.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Consumer spending growth slowed from about 6.8% in September but remains positive and above the 4.50% trailing 12-month pace.
Discretionary growth is running below non-discretionary growth, led by slower hobby, home and travel spending.
Essentials spending is firm, supported by higher energy costs.
Excluding gas stations the slowdown is sharper, so energy prices are propping up the headline.

macro_indicators.indicator: Chase gasoline and other energy goods spending Y/Y (MTD)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Spending at gas stations is accelerating on much higher pump prices, a headwind for lower and middle income consumers.

macro_indicators.indicator: Average US gas price Y/Y (JPMorgan estimate)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Prices are roughly flat from September's ~$4.35 but far above last year, which squeezes lower-income budgets.

risk_factors: Higher pump prices act as a regressive tax on lower and middle income consumers.
Discretionary spending is slowing broadly, across income and age cohorts, in hobby, home and travel categories.
Calendar shifts such as the Labor Day weekend moving into September may distort the month-over-month comparison.

theme_stances.evidence: Total spending growth in October is lower M/M vs. September.
